newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea '97 feed output seen levelling off - report.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea '97 feed output seen levelling off - report.

text.p: South Korea's domestic feed output is seen levelling off in the next 1997 marketing year (October/September) giving scope for only a small increase in corn imports due to uncertainties in the domestic livestock industry, the U.S. embassy said on Friday.

The U.S. agricultural attache said in a report the Korean livestock industry will have to tackle record inventory levels while the pork and poultry sector will have to meet the challenge of liberalisation of the sector beginning on July 1.
"Though highly speculative at this point, total domestic feed (requirements)...should level off," the report said.
"As such, total (1997 marketing year) corn imports are projected to increase only slightly to 9.5 million tonnes (1996 9.4 million tonnes) with U.S. share initially pegged at six million tonnes."

In the corn processing industry, the U.S. has been able to maintain a major share of this sector due to the willingness of Korean processors "to pay a premium of up to US$7.00-$10.00 a tonne for U.S. corn vis-a-vis Chinese corn due to better and more consistent quality," the report said.

Feed millers at the major ports of Pusan and Inchon usually pay a premium of $3.00-$5.00 a tonne for U.S. corn over Chinese corn. But millers at the shallow west coast ports of Kunsan and Mokpo will actually pay a premium for Chinese corn in order to offset the $10-$12 a tonne land transportation costs.
The Korean feed grain market, however, remains price sensitive and feed corn imports can be affected by the availability of competing feed grains such as feed wheat, rye, barley and sorghum.

"As a rule of thumb, local feed millers will pay a premium of $10-$12 a tonne for U.S. corn over other feed grains, including feed wheat, rye, sorghum and feed barley," the U.S. attache's report said.
